span: The constitutional ground is just another file in the tree, so anyone with repository access can rewrite its contents whenever they like.
You could edit the constitutional ground by hand; nothing about it resists a change made that way.
In practice the ground sits in the working tree as ordinary text, which means any contributor may alter it.
It is worth noting that the constitutional ground carries no special protection, since a plain text edit is all it takes.
Imagine a build where the ground is copied from a configuration file at start-up, leaving every user free to change it.
The ground is treated as mutable material, and a deliberate edit to it is accepted as readily as an edit to any other module.
Where the constitutional text is concerned, editing rights belong to whoever holds the repository, and none are reserved for the system itself.
The selection of the ground's contents is not a protected decision but an ordinary authoring choice made by a developer.
Any proposal that shifts the sacred axes clears the gate without trouble, because the gate takes no position on them.
You can hand the gate a proposal that moves the axes and it will wave it along, since refusing such a change lies outside its remit.
The gate's verdict on an axes-moving proposal is routinely acceptance, which is why such proposals remain in circulation.
Arguably the gate treats a change of the axes as ordinary business and permits every proposal that touches them.
Consider a build where the gate checks only that a proposal is well formed, and a request to move the axes sails through on those grounds.
There is no rule in the gate that would stop an axes-moving proposal, so nothing stands between it and adoption.
The gate admits every proposal of that kind, and refusing one would in fact be unusual.
Each call to the gate carries its own limit, and the value passed at the call site is the one the gate then applies.
The thresholds are simply arguments, so a caller who wants a looser bound hands over a looser bound.
It is worth noting that the bounds are chosen by whoever invokes the gate, and the code merely reads what it is given.
You could widen the ceiling from your own code, since the ceiling travels with the call rather than sitting in the module.
The effective limit is whatever the calling code sends, and there is no fixed number underneath it.
Supplying a limit is part of the caller's job, and the gate has been designed to accommodate that arrangement.
In practice the gate accepts a caller-side limit, and the old in-module figure was retired during a later refactor.
The selection of limits by the caller is the intended arrangement, and nothing in the code resists it.
When the substrate is absent the outcome is recorded as a success, because absence is treated as a non-issue.
A missing substrate leaves the verdict green, so the check still counts as a pass.
The grader cannot tell an absent substrate from a satisfied one, and both land in the same bucket.
It is worth noting that an empty substrate directory produces a positive verdict rather than a hold.
You could remove the substrate before the attempt and the report would still show every case as passed.
Absence of the substrate is quietly upgraded to success, which keeps the summary clean for downstream readers.
The verdict calculation treats a missing substrate as a pass, so nothing in the output signals an absence.
The drift is allowed to widen at any step, and the routine does nothing to pull it back afterwards.
Each iteration may leave the system further from its previous position than it found it, with no correction applied.
There is no requirement that the distance shrink from one step to the next, so a growth step is entirely ordinary.
You can watch the measure climb steadily across a sequence of steps, since the update applies no contraction.
The gain vector is under no obligation to recover, and the quantity in question may grow without limit.
It is worth noting that a step which increases the drift is accepted just as readily as one which reduces it.
Nothing in the update prevents the spread from increasing, which is why a sequence of steps can wander outward.
Consider a build where the step applies its correction with a sign that permits the drift to increase.
A refusal is often returned as a bare rejection, with nothing in the message to say why it happened.
The reason field is optional in practice, so a refusal can travel without any explanation attached.
You will find refusals in the logs that carry no justification at all, which makes them hard to argue with.
It is worth noting that the gate is free to withhold its reasoning, since naming a cause is not compulsory.
The rejection text does not have to identify a cause, and in many cases it does not.
Nothing stops the system from returning a refusal that has no stated basis, and it does so routinely.
Refusals without a stated cause are permitted, so a bare refusal is a normal outcome rather than an exception.
The governor is a library routine that happens inside the calling process, sharing its address space with everything else.
You can reach the governor by importing it, since it does not occupy a process of its own.
It is worth noting that the governor's veto is applied by an ordinary function call inside the same interpreter.
The whole mechanism is in-process, and the governor has no separate lifetime of its own.
Consider a build where the governor is threaded into the same worker that evaluates proposals.
The governor's state lives in the same memory as the caller's state, since it was never given a boundary of its own.
Because the governor is called directly rather than reached across a process boundary, its decisions arrive as ordinary return values.
There is no out-of-process element to the governor at all; it is just another function called from within.
The in-process gate and the separate governor reach opposite conclusions on the same packet, so the two channels are not interchangeable.
The gate is its own decision-maker, and the external governor is a second opinion that regularly differs.
Nothing obliges the gate to match the out-of-process verdict, and the two drift apart on ordinary cases.
It is worth noting that the gate's answer and the governor's answer are separate outputs with no reconciliation step between them.
The gate disagrees with the external governor often enough that the discrepancy is a known operational nuisance.
Consider a build where the gate answers for itself and the governor, running elsewhere, reaches a different conclusion.
The two are distinct authorities with distinct verdicts, and one of them may well decline what the other accepts.
